title: Four Systems, Four Ways of Living
body: A photograph and a question
In 1945, an American military photographer took a famous photograph at the liberation of Buchenwald. Survivors stood among wooden bunks, reduced to skin and bone, staring hollow-eyed into the camera.

That same year, on the other side of the Pacific, a Japanese aircraft carrying a twenty-year-old man flew straight toward an American warship. Before leaving, he had written to his mother, saying he was honored to give his life for the emperor.
On the Eastern Front, Soviet soldiers fell by the thousand each day on the road to Berlin. Their generals showed little concern for the number: there were more men behind them to fill the gaps.
In the United States, a hundred and twenty thousand Japanese Americans were still held in incarceration camps. Most were American citizens. Many had sons fighting in Europe in American uniform.

Four scenes, four different ways of making people cease to be ends. If the Second World War were simply a story of “good and evil,” the first scene would be enough. Together, the four reveal something more complex and more important: every major participant in the war used people as means in different ways. The differences lay not in whether they did so, but in how, how profoundly, and, most importantly, whether they could turn back.
Nazi Germany: when “not human” became a category
The Nazi system's distinctiveness lay not simply in brutality; history contains no shortage of regimes more brutal than it. It lay in its industrial precision.

Auschwitz was not only a prison, not only an execution ground, but a factory. Raw materials, human beings, were transported in; sorted, with those able to work retained and others sent straight to gas chambers; put on production lines of forced labor until exhaustion; and finally disposed of by burning. There were schedules, quotas, and quality controls. The railway administration dispatched both passenger and freight cars for deportations and charged by the number of people and the distance traveled.

This was more dehumanizing than madness: it was madness in a rationalized form. After removing people from the category of “human,” this “rationality” managed extermination as it would manage a factory.

Turning psychological impulses into industrialized murder required something else: an institutional order that would not object. Every dimension of the Nazi system was designed to make dissent impossible. Information had a single source, the state propaganda machine. Power flowed in one direction, down from the Führer. There was no feedback loop: if the front was failing, the fault lay with frontline commanders, never with the strategy.

In such a system, even a person who sensed that something was wrong had no channel for bringing that feeling into institutional decisions. Conscience became a private matter, institutionally irrelevant. A few brave people, the White Rose resistance and those behind the July 20 plot against Hitler, confronted the system at the cost of their lives and failed to overthrow it. This was not because Germans lacked consciences, but because the system's design destroyed the pathways through which conscience could act.
The Soviet Union: fuel for history

The Soviet Union and Nazi Germany were mortal enemies. Yet they bore a strange resemblance in one respect: both treated individuals as raw material for a greater undertaking. The difference lay in the nature of that undertaking.

The Nazi project was spatial: Lebensraum, a racial empire, a thousand-year Reich. These concepts pointed toward an ultimate geographical and biological condition. The Soviet project was temporal: historical progress, the eventual realization of communism. Its goal remained forever in the future, forever on a horizon marked “just one more step.”

Soviet casualties in the Battle of Stalingrad exceeded a million. In the logic criticized here, Zhukov's tactics did not take the soldier's life as their unit of account. A height might change hands more than a dozen times, hundreds or thousands falling each time before the next wave filled their place. Such an attitude toward life was more than tactical crudity. It reflected an underlying logic: individual lives were fuel for history. If theory had already established history's direction, if communism must arrive, then the fuel consumed in accelerating that journey counted as a legitimate cost.

This instrumentalization also carried a distinctive problem: it had no point of completion. The Nazi racial empire had, in theory, a finished state, however nightmarish. Communism remained “not yet.” “Sacrifice a little more” could therefore always be justified. The next intermediate goal was waiting as soon as the previous one had been reached.

A perpetual-motion demand, with nobody ever able to say “enough.” Saying “enough” meant questioning the direction of history; questioning that direction meant counterrevolution. On this reading, Soviet purges were not simply the product of Stalin's personal paranoia, though he was paranoid. They were a regular function of a system that continually demanded “more sacrifice,” and therefore had to identify and remove those “unwilling to sacrifice.”
Japan: when death became the end itself

Japanese militarism is usually placed in the same narrative frame as Nazi Germany: fascism, aggression, atrocity. These labels are justified, but they can conceal something distinctive about the Japanese model.

On June 6, 1945, during the Battle of Okinawa, Rear Admiral Minoru Ōta sent a telegram to Tokyo before his suicide, describing the terrible suffering of Okinawan civilians. Yet his conclusion was not “Please stop this war,” but a plea that the Okinawan people be treated with consideration. Within his framework, the war itself was beyond question, because it extended from the kokutai, the national polity, which was sacred. The manner of carrying it out could be questioned; its direction could not.

Many letters that kamikaze pilots wrote to their families before departure reveal fear, reluctance to part, even doubt. Yet almost none refused to fly. Not because they would be executed, although refusal could indeed have serious consequences, but because, in the worldview they had been taught, dying for the emperor was not sacrifice but fulfillment. Life reached its highest meaning at the moment it was offered to the national polity.

This was a distinctive form of instrumentalization. The Nazis classified certain people as “not human” in order to destroy them. The Soviet system treated people as “fuel for history” to be consumed. Japanese militarism did something more unsettling: it redefined the meaning of an “end,” presenting death not as a cost imposed on a person, but as the highest form of self-realization.

When death is encoded as self-realization, resistance becomes logically impossible within that code. To resist is to refuse fulfillment; to refuse fulfillment is to deny the meaning of one's own existence. The system need not rely on violence to sustain such a condition. Individuals carry out its demands themselves because they sincerely believe that this is their own purpose.

This internalized instrumentalization is difficult to break merely by removing external coercion. Postwar transformation in both Germany and Japan was prolonged and uneven: institutional reform, changes in social attitudes, and the reckoning with responsibility for the war were different processes, and they did not reach completion at the same time. What needed to change was not only a set of external institutions, but also the ways people understood their relationship with the state.
Britain and America: possibilities in the cracks

Now comes the hardest part to write. The problems of Nazism, the Soviet system, and Japanese militarism are relatively easy to identify. Their logics of instrumentalization differ, but all are extreme. Britain and America are more complicated because they combine two real things: instrumentalization and the possibility of correction.

First, the instrumentalization. In February 1942, Roosevelt signed Executive Order 9066, authorizing the removal that led to Japanese Americans on the West Coast being forced into inland incarceration camps. A hundred and twenty thousand people, two-thirds of them American citizens. They had not been charged with crimes or tried in court. Ancestry alone cost them their freedom. Fred Korematsu was arrested on a street corner in San Leandro for refusing the removal order. His case reached the Supreme Court, which in 1944 upheld the exclusion order by six votes to three: national security overrode individual rights.

In Britain, Churchill approved large-scale bombing of German cities. In February 1945, Dresden suffered successive air raids. According to the city’s historical commission, approximately eighteen to twenty-five thousand people died, the great majority civilians. The military necessity remains disputed. Then there was the Bengal famine of 1943, which killed between two and three million people. The disruption of war, rising prices, failures in food distribution, and other factors combined to cause the disaster; the wartime policies and failures of relief of the British colonial authorities made it worse.

The Japanese American camps, Dresden, the Bengal famine: up to this point, the logic in Britain and America was not fundamentally different from that of the other three systems. People were used as means. What happened next was different.

Korematsu lost his case. But he did not disappear. He survived, kept speaking, kept challenging. Forty years later, in 1983, a federal court overturned his conviction. In 1988, President Reagan signed the Civil Liberties Act, offering an official apology and compensation for the incarceration of Japanese Americans.

The bombing of Dresden remains a live subject of British public debate. Anniversaries renew the argument: legitimate military operation or war crime? There is no settled answer, but the point is that disagreement is permitted. Memory of the Bengal famine played an important role in India's independence movement, and responsibility continues to be examined in postcolonial scholarship.

Was correction slow? Extremely. Incomplete? Deeply. Full of hypocrisy? Of course. Taking forty years to overturn an unjust conviction is nothing to boast about. Yet correction could occur because the British and American systems contained some underlying features absent from the other three: information could circulate through multiple channels; power did not run only one way; feedback loops existed; and membership was nominally universal.

“All men are created equal” was never fully realized in practice. But as a norm the system had already accepted, anyone could invoke it against the system's own conduct. This is precisely what Martin Luther King Jr. later did. He was not overthrowing the American order. He was telling it, “Your own principles say that everyone is equal. Please honor them.” Those words had force because the system did acknowledge the principle.

In Nazi Germany, “You promised Aryan supremacy, but you are sacrificing Aryans” carried no force, because the system did not recognize any individual “Aryan” as having value independent of race. In the Soviet Union, saying “You promised to serve the people, but the people are hungry” could be treated as counterrevolutionary. Within Japanese militarism's conceptual framework, “The national polity demands our deaths, but I do not want to die” could not even count as a valid argument.
Only when a system's basic rules contain a commitment to people as ends, however incompletely honored, does correction have a point of departure.
Where the difference lies
Putting the four systems side by side yields something more useful than a binary division between “good” and “bad”: why can some systems correct themselves while others cannot?

The answer is not in ideals. Soviet ideals also claimed to serve the people; Japanese imperial ideals also proclaimed the emperor's care for his subjects. Ideals can say anything. The answer lies deeper, in the system's underlying structure:

Does information have only one source? Does power flow only one way? When something goes wrong, can that information return to the people making decisions? Is the answer to “Who counts as human?” fixed, or can it change?

The Nazi answers were: information must have one source; power must flow downward; there must be no feedback channel; and who counts as human is fixed. Japanese militarism offered the same answers, even internalizing questions of human standing within individual psychology. The Soviet answers to the first three were much the same. Only the last was nominally changeable, though in practice the center of power decided it.

The British and American answers were: information does “not entirely” have one source; power does “not entirely” flow downward; feedback mechanisms exist “but” are often ignored; membership in humanity is nominally universal “and” that promise can be invoked.

These qualifications sound weak. Beside the absolute closure of the other three systems, however, even the cracks in British and American institutions look like open doors. Fortunately, history tells us that cracks can be enough.

A system need not perfectly treat people as ends; such perfection may never be attainable through institutions alone. What it needs are cracks: informational cracks through which dissent can spread, institutional cracks through which power can be challenged, feedback cracks through which errors can be identified, and conceptual cracks through which “Who counts as human?” can be answered anew.

People do not become ends simply because an institution declares them to be. They become ends again and again within those cracks, through struggle, speech, and correction. This is not a condition that can be achieved once and for all. It is a process that must continue.
deck: Wartime systems differed not only in how they used people, but in whether people could challenge and correct them.
